id: Man's Short Life and Foolish Ambition

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

O man, O man, what high ambition growsWithin his brain, and yet how low he goes!To be contented only with a sound,Wherein is neither peace nor life nor body found.

Keywords: How, With, Saw

outputs.L1:
In gardens sweet, each flower marked I well—  
How it would spring, bud, bloom, then fade and die.  
Thus, contemplating man’s brief earthly stay,  
I saw him, like those flowers, pass away.  

Yet houses thick and strong and high he builds,  
As though he were to live eternally.  
He hoards a mass of wealth, yet cannot fill  
His empty mind, but covets ever still.  
To gain or keep it, falsehood he will use;  
Wrong, right, or truth—no base means will refuse.  

I would not blame him, could he death repel,  
Ease all his pains, or rest secure in sleep;  
Or purchase Heaven’s mansions, like the gods become,  
And with his gold rule stars and moon and sun;  
Command the winds to blow, the seas obey,  
Level their waves, and bid the breezes stay.  

But he no power has, except to die,  
And care throughout his life is misery.  
This care is but a word, an empty sound,  
Wherein nor soul nor substance can be found;  
Yet as his heir he makes it to inherit,  
And all he has he leaves unto this spirit.  

To gain this Child of Fame, this barren word,  
He fears no danger—neither fire nor sword.  
All horrid pains and death he will endure,  
Or anything, if only fame he may procure.  

O man, O man, what lofty ambition grows  
Within his mind—and yet how low he goes!  
Contented only with an empty sound,  
Where neither peace, nor life, nor substance can be found.
outputs.L2:
While walking through a garden, I observed each bloom  
rise from the earth, form a bud, open, fade, and perish.  
Reflecting on how briefly human beings remain alive,  
I saw that people vanish just as flowers do.

Even so, a man constructs tall, solid, crowded buildings  
as though he expects to endure forever.  
He gathers immense riches, but they cannot satisfy him;  
his restless heart continues craving more.  
To acquire or preserve his wealth, he resorts to deceit,  
rejecting neither injustice nor any other shameful method.

I would not condemn him if money could prevent his death,  
relieve his suffering, or guarantee peaceful sleep;  
if it could purchase him a home in Heaven, make him divine,  
or let him govern the stars, the moon, and the sun;  
if gold enabled him to direct the winds, command the oceans,  
flatten their waves, or still every breeze.

But he possesses no such power—only the capacity to die—  
and all his anxious striving makes life miserable.  
The worldly reputation he pursues is merely a word,  
an empty noise without soul or substance.  
Nevertheless, he treats it as his successor,  
leaving everything he owns to this insubstantial legacy.

To obtain this offspring of ambition called Fame,  
he will face every danger, whether flame or blade.  
He is prepared to suffer terrible agony and even death,  
or endure anything else, provided he wins renown.

O humanity, how lofty the ambition conceived in the mind,  
and yet how far it lowers those who follow it!  
A person finally settles for nothing more than a sound—  
something containing no peace, no life, and no physical reality.
outputs.L3:
The speaker compares human life to the brief existence of flowers: people spring into life, flourish for a short time, then wither and die. Yet despite knowing how fleeting life is, they build grand houses and accumulate wealth as if they were destined to live forever. Their desire for possessions often grows into greed, leading them to use deception and commit wrongdoing in order to gain riches or protect what they already own.

However, wealth offers no defense against life’s greatest realities. It cannot prevent death, relieve the deepest forms of human suffering, or give anyone control over nature, time, or eternity. Material possessions therefore provide only an illusion of security and power. The pursuit of fame is equally misguided. People willingly endure danger, pain, and even death to make their names widely known, yet fame is ultimately nothing more than an empty and insubstantial name. Through these reflections, the speaker exposes the vanity of seeking permanence through wealth or reputation in a life that is inevitably brief.
outputs.L4:
Watching flowers bloom in beauty and then quickly wither, the speaker is reminded of the brevity of human life. Like blossoms, people flourish for only a short time before age and death overtake them. Yet despite knowing that life is temporary, humanity devotes enormous energy to acquiring wealth, securing power, and winning public admiration. People struggle to protect themselves from uncertainty and to create reputations that might survive them, as though material success or fame could offer lasting safety.

The speaker exposes the futility of these ambitions. Wealth cannot prevent death, security is always fragile, and fame leaves behind only a name—an empty echo that cannot benefit the person who has died. Worse, the pursuit of such rewards often produces fear, restlessness, and moral compromise. The ambitious person sacrifices honesty, contentment, and inner peace for achievements that are temporary and ultimately powerless.

By contrasting human striving with the natural cycle of flowers, the poem reveals the folly of living as though worldly success could overcome mortality. Its message is not simply that death is unavoidable, but that awareness of death should lead people to reconsider what they value. Integrity and peace are more meaningful than riches or reputation because they shape the quality of life itself. To surrender them for possessions, status, or remembrance is to exchange something real and lasting in the present for promises that cannot protect anyone from life’s inevitable end.
outputs.L5:
### How, With, Saw

“How did you build it?” Mia asked.

“With patience,” her grandfather replied, holding up an old saw. Together, they cut and shaped the wood until it became a small boat.

When they placed it on the lake, Mia saw it glide across the water. She finally understood how simple tools, when used with care, could turn an idea into something real.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Renaissance-style poem about the brevity of human life, comparing people to flowers and condemning greed, ambition, and the pursuit of fame.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Mortal Flower**

As doth the rose at dawn her red display,  
And ere the evensong her beauty vail,  
So mortal flesh puts forth its pride to-day,  
To-morrow bowed beneath the winter’s gale.  

Yet Avarice heaps gold, though gold breeds rust,  
And proud Ambition scales a tottering throne;  
Fame sounds her brazen trumpet o’er the dust,  
Then leaves the vaunted name unheard, unknown.  

O fools, who sell life’s little noon for gain,  
And wound the soul to win the crowd’s acclaim!  
Death reaps alike the monarch and the swain,  
And Time’s cold breath puts out the brightest name.  

Then sow sweet love while yet thy flower is fair:  
This bloom survives when crowns dissolve to air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming philosophical poem in archaic English that reflects on mortality, wealth, worldly power, and humanity’s futile desire to leave a famous name behind.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Name Upon the Dust**

O mortal wight, why heap thy hoard,  
And bind thy heart to yellow gold?  
Death heedeth not the rich man’s board,  
Nor spareth prince for wealth untold.  

The king may lift his sceptre high,  
And bid the trembling nations kneel;  
Yet Time, whose wing none may deny,  
Shall rust his crown and blunt his steel.  

Thy towers may pierce the vaulted blue,  
Thy banners mock the morning flame;  
But rain shall wash each stone anew,  
And silence swallow up thy name.  

“Remember me!” frail mankind saith,  
And carveth praise on marble cold;  
Yet every letter yieldeth breath,  
And every storied deed grows old.  

Where now the lords of ages fled,  
Whose trumpets shook the field and throne?  
The worm keepeth counsel with the dead,  
And dust claimeth each as bone to bone.  

Then boast thee not of purse or might,  
Nor crave that Fame thy worth rehearse;  
Do mercy whilst thou hast the light—  
A kindly deed outliveth verse.  

For man is but a candle’s gleam,  
A shadow cast, a passing breath;  
His glory, like a winter dream,  
Awaketh in the arms of Death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in heroic couplets beginning with observations of flowers budding and dying, then use that image to criticize people who build houses and hoard riches as though they were immortal.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the rose unseals her crimson room,  
By dusk, her scattered rubies strew the gloom.  

The lilies lift their chalices to day,  
Then bow their pallid foreheads to decay.  

Bud follows bloom, and bloom resigns its breath;  
The garden keeps its calendar of death.  

Yet men lay stone on stone and call it stay,  
Though Time already gnaws the beams away.  

With cedar roofs they bargain against Fate,  
While worms, unbribed, attend them at the gate.  

They bolt their gold where sunlight cannot shine,  
And praise the guarded darkness: “Mine, all mine.”  

They starve today to glut some unborn heir;  
The grave admits no ledger, lock, or care.  

They build for centuries, though made of hours,  
And scorn the sermon spoken by the flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a seventeenth-century-style meditation on how humans cannot conquer death, command nature, purchase Heaven, or gain lasting happiness through gold and ambition.
counterfactuals.output:
### A Meditation upon Man’s False Dominion

O Man, thou little monarch of an hour, who carriest a sceptre of dust and callest the shadow thine inheritance, consider how narrow is thy kingdom. Thou mayest fortify thy chamber, summon physicians, and fill thy coffers against the evil day; yet Death entereth without knocking. He respecteth neither the purple robe nor the beggar’s rag, but maketh one silence of princes and prisoners. The sword cannot wound him, nor policy deceive him, nor tears persuade him to tarry.

Neither canst thou command Nature, though for a season she suffer thy hand upon the bridle. Thou mayest bank the river, yet the flood remembereth its ancient road; thou mayest sow the field, but not compel the cloud; thou mayest chart the sea, but not still its anger. The wind receiveth no commission from kings, and the thunder sealeth no covenant with captains. He that boasteth, “The earth obeyeth me,” is answered by an earthquake beneath his feet.

Think not, moreover, that Heaven is a province to be purchased. Gold may open the gates of palaces, but it hath no key for Paradise. No jewel can bribe the Judge, nor can a rich man hire another to repent in his stead. The coin that beareth Caesar’s image must remain with Caesar; the soul beareth another Image, and unto its Maker must it return.

Why then dost thou climb the icy hill of Ambition, where every step increaseth thy danger and diminisheth thy rest? Honour is a trumpet sounded by another’s breath; Fame, an echo that outliveth neither the valley nor the hearer. Riches promise warmth, yet breed a colder hunger; for he who possesseth much commonly desireth more, and so becometh servant to that which he nameth his treasure.

Seek not, therefore, a lasting joy among things appointed to perish. Gold rusteth in the heart before it rusteth in the chest. Crowns press heavily upon the brow, and garlands wither even while they are worn. Make peace with thy mortality; receive Nature as a steward, not a tyrant; use wealth as a traveller useth a staff, but worship it not as a god. For man’s true greatness consisteth not in conquering Death, but in learning how to die; not in commanding the world, but in governing himself; not in buying Heaven, but in becoming fit to desire it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an extended moral poem addressing “O man, O man,” arguing that fame is merely an empty sound without peace, life, soul, or substance.
counterfactuals.output:
**O Man, O Man**

O man, O man, why dost thou climb  
The trembling battlements of Time,  
And carve thy name with anxious hand  
Upon the frail and shifting sand?  
The wind that flatters thee today  
Tomorrow bears thy trace away;  
And Fame, whose trumpet shakes the crowd,  
Is but an empty breath made loud.

What peace is in the brazen call  
That wakes the ear and startles all?  
Can echoes soothe the sleepless breast,  
Or praise command the heart to rest?  
Though every tongue repeat thy name,  
Thou mayst be cold within thy fame;  
For noise may fill the courts of kings,  
Yet silence dwells beneath its wings.

O man, O man, the laurel leaf  
Can neither heal nor comfort grief.  
It cannot cool the fevered head,  
Nor summon back the cherished dead;  
It cannot make the guilty whole,  
Nor pour forgiveness through the soul.  
Its green is brief, its fragrance slight—  
A wreath by day, dry dust by night.

What life is in the sculptured stone  
That guards a glory not its own?  
The marble face, the gilded name,  
Are senseless ministers of fame.  
They neither breathe, nor love, nor know  
The living joy, the living woe;  
And monuments, though proudly raised,  
Feel not the praise of those who praised.

O man, O man, suppose the earth  
Should ring from pole to pole thy worth;  
Suppose thy victories were told  
By countless mouths, in letters gold;  
If in thy chamber, lone and deep,  
Thy conscience will not let thee sleep,  
What profit brings the world’s acclaim?  
A wounded heart outlives a name.

For Fame has neither blood nor breath,  
Nor hand to save the soul from death;  
No pulse within her trumpet lies,  
No tender light within her eyes.  
She cannot sit beside thy bed,  
Nor break one loaf, nor bow one head;  
She cannot clasp thee when afraid—  
A painted fire, a hollow shade.

The crowd that lifts thee like a star  
Will scatter when new wonders are.  
The lips that cried thy praises high  
Will learn another name to cry.  
As waves that glitter, break, and cease,  
Their clamor knows no root in peace;  
And he who builds his joy thereon  
Builds on a sea—and soon is gone.

O man, O man, seek not thy worth  
In passing judgments of the earth.  
A thousand voices, joined as one,  
Cannot create a second sun;  
Nor can their scorn extinguish light  
That burns in truth before the night.  
The just are rich though none applaud;  
The false are poor though crowned abroad.

Better one quiet deed of grace,  
Unseen by any human face;  
Better one cup to thirst supplied,  
One mourner comforted beside;  
Better one enemy forgiven,  
Than all the thunder under heaven  
That shouts thy triumph through the air,  
Then leaves thee emptier than despair.

Better a conscience clean and still  
Than banners flying on the hill;  
Better a lowly room with peace  
Than palaces where praises cease;  
Better one faithful friend who stays  
Than multitudes with borrowed praise;  
Better one hour of love’s true breath  
Than ages of renown in death.

For what is Fame when flesh is clay,  
And all her heralds pass away?  
A syllable the living lend  
To one who cannot hear its end;  
A fading circle on the stream,  
A bell heard dimly in a dream;  
A footprint where the tides advance,  
A shadow crowned by circumstance.

No soul inhabits her applause;  
She neither loves, nor wills, nor draws.  
No substance fills her splendid shell;  
Her courts are wide, but none may dwell.  
She promises immortal bloom,  
Yet cannot cross the narrow tomb;  
And all the immortality  
She gives is dust in memory.

O man, O man, then turn thine eyes  
From smoky praise and painted skies.  
Let truth, not rumor, be thy guide;  
Let mercy walk at wisdom’s side.  
Do good because the good is fair,  
Not that the world may see thee there;  
And when thy right hand gives the bread,  
Let vanity bow down its head.

Make peace thy crown, and love thy throne;  
Call no possession all thine own.  
Keep life within thy daily deed,  
And soul within thy word and creed.  
Then, though thy name be never sung,  
Nor praised by pen, nor borne by tongue,  
Thou shalt possess what Fame denied:  
A quiet heart, a life inside.

And when the final dusk is near,  
No trumpet shall be needed there.  
The kindness sown, the burden shared,  
The truth maintained, the wrong repaired—  
These shall not sound, but they shall be;  
Not echoes, but reality.  
Their substance shall outlast the breath  
Of clamorous praise and conquer death.

O man, O man, be warned in time:  
Fame is an echo, not a chime;  
A vacant sound, a restless flame,  
A mask that has no living name.  
Without true peace, it is but strife;  
Without good works, it has no life;  
Without love’s soul, no light is won;  
Without truth’s substance—it is none.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
